item.title: Branching in Glucose Polymers and the Rate of Glucose Release
item.stimulus:
Students compare two glucose storage polymers. Each is made only of glucose monomers.

- Polymer L is a single unbranched chain of 600 glucose units, so it has one chain end that an enzyme can act on.
- Polymer B is a branched polymer of the same total mass. Its many branches give it 40 chain ends.

The students add the same concentration of an enzyme to separate tubes, one containing each polymer, at 37 °C and pH 7. The enzyme removes glucose monomers one at a time, and only from the free end of a chain. The substrate is in excess throughout the experiment. The students measure the total glucose released.

Time (min) | Glucose released from L (µmol) | Glucose released from B (µmol)
0 | 0 | 0
5 | 4 | 60
10 | 8 | 120
item.model_answer:
(a) Both polymers are built from glucose, a monosaccharide. Each pair of glucose monomers is joined by a covalent bond. The bond forms by dehydration synthesis, in which one water molecule is removed for each bond made.

(b) In an unbranched chain of 600 monomers, there are 600 − 1 = 599 bonds. Each bond releases one water molecule, so 599 water molecules are released.

(c) Polymer L: 8 µmol ÷ 10 min = 0.8 µmol/min.
Polymer B: 120 µmol ÷ 10 min = 12 µmol/min.
12 ÷ 0.8 = 15, so glucose is released 15 times faster from Polymer B.

(d) The enzyme removes glucose only from free chain ends. Because Polymer B is branched, it has 40 chain ends compared with only 1 for Polymer L. Many enzyme molecules can therefore hydrolyze glucose from Polymer B at the same time, which increases the rate of release.

Prediction: an animal whose glycogen has far fewer branches would release glucose from glycogen more slowly during exercise. Fewer branches mean fewer chain ends where enzymes can remove glucose, so less glucose would be made available per minute when the animal needs it.

item.title: Branching and Glucose Release from Storage Polysaccharides
item.stimulus:
Many organisms store energy as polysaccharides built from glucose. Polysaccharide L is an unbranched (linear) chain of glucose. Polysaccharide B is made of the same glucose monomers joined by the same covalent bonds, but its chains are highly branched, so each molecule has many free chain ends.

Students studied an enzyme that releases glucose from storage polysaccharides. The enzyme hydrolyzes only the bond holding the last glucose at a free chain end. It cannot cut bonds in the interior of a chain. Students prepared two tubes, each containing 10 mg of one polysaccharide in buffer at the same pH and temperature. They added the same amount of enzyme to each tube, in excess. After 10 minutes they measured the free glucose in each tube.

Tube | Polysaccharide | Free glucose after 10 min (µmol)
1 | L (linear) | 15
2 | B (branched) | 90
item.model_answer:
(a) Each glucose monomer is joined to the next by a covalent bond formed by dehydration synthesis. When the bond forms, an H from one monomer and an OH from the other are removed as one water molecule, so one water is released for every bond made. Repeating this builds the polymer.

(b) A linear chain of 1,200 glucose monomers has 1,200 − 1 = 1,199 covalent bonds between monomers. Hydrolysis breaks each bond by adding one water molecule, so 1,199 water molecules are required.

(c) 90 µmol ÷ 15 µmol = 6, so polysaccharide B released 6 times as much glucose. Polysaccharide B is highly branched, so each molecule has many free chain ends, while linear polysaccharide L has only one usable end per molecule. Because the enzyme can remove glucose only from a chain end and was present in excess, the number of chain ends limited the rate. With many more ends, many enzyme molecules can hydrolyze glucose off polysaccharide B at the same time, so glucose is released faster.

(d) The mutant animal will release glucose from its stores more slowly than a normal animal. Its storage polysaccharide has only long linear chains, so there are far fewer chain ends where enzymes can hydrolyze glucose off, just as linear polysaccharide L released less glucose than branched polysaccharide B. During intense exercise its cells would get glucose from stores more slowly.

item.title: Glucose Release from Linear and Branched Polysaccharides
item.stimulus:
A student compares two storage polysaccharides, X and Y, each built entirely from glucose monomers. Polysaccharide X is an unbranched (linear) chain. Polysaccharide Y has many branch points, so each molecule has many chain ends. The student adds equal masses of X and Y to separate tubes of buffer at the same temperature and pH. An equal amount of the same enzyme is added to each tube. The enzyme removes one glucose at a time and can act only at the free end of a chain. The enzyme is in excess, so every available chain end is acted on. The student measures the total glucose released over 20 minutes.

Time (min) | Glucose released from X (µmol) | Glucose released from Y (µmol)
0 | 0 | 0
5 | 4 | 20
10 | 8 | 40
15 | 12 | 60
20 | 16 | 80
item.model_answer:
(a) Each polysaccharide is a polymer of glucose monomers (monosaccharides) joined to one another by covalent bonds, formed by dehydration synthesis. The enzyme catalyzes hydrolysis: it adds a water molecule across the covalent bond between the last glucose and the rest of the chain, breaking the bond and releasing one glucose.

(b) X: (16 − 0) µmol ÷ (20 − 0) min = 0.8 µmol/min. Y: (80 − 0) µmol ÷ 20 min = 4.0 µmol/min.

(c) Polysaccharide Y is branched, so each molecule has many chain ends, while linear X has few ends. Because the enzyme can remove glucose only from a free end and is in excess, many enzyme molecules work at the many ends of Y simultaneously. More sites of hydrolysis at once means glucose is released faster from Y, which is 5 times faster than from X.

(d) The animal will release glucose from storage more slowly. Without branch points its storage polymer consists of linear chains with far fewer chain ends, so fewer sites are available at the same time for enzymes that remove glucose from ends, just as linear X released glucose more slowly than branched Y.

ry=F(y[-1]-y[0],t[-1]-t[0])
assert rx==F(4,5)
assert abs(float(rx)-0.8)<1e-9
assert ry==4
assert ry/rx==5
for i in range(1,5):
    assert F(x[i],t[i])==rx and F(y[i],t[i])==ry
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

item.title: Hydrolysis of Linear and Branched Glucose Polymers
item.stimulus:
A researcher studies two polysaccharides isolated from different organisms. Each molecule of either polysaccharide contains exactly 1,200 monomers. Polymer L is a single unbranched (linear) chain. Polymer B is highly branched. When either polymer is completely broken down, the only product is glucose.

The researcher also has enzyme X. Enzyme X removes one glucose monomer at a time, and it can act only at the free end of a chain. Each molecule of polymer L has 1 chain end that enzyme X can act on. Each molecule of polymer B has 40 chain ends that enzyme X can act on.

The researcher prepares two test tubes. Each tube contains the same mass of polysaccharide, the same amount of enzyme X, and the same buffer at the same temperature. Tube 1 contains polymer L. Tube 2 contains polymer B. The amount of free glucose in each tube is measured after 5 minutes.
item.model_answer:
(a) Both polymers are made of glucose, a monosaccharide (simple sugar). The glucose monomers are joined to each other by covalent bonds, which form during dehydration synthesis.

(b) Polymer L is a linear chain of 1,200 glucose monomers, so it contains 1,200 − 1 = 1,199 covalent bonds between monomers. Hydrolysis breaks each bond by adding one water molecule (H to one monomer, OH to the other). Complete hydrolysis therefore requires 1,199 water molecules.

(c) Tube 2, which contains the branched polymer B, will contain more free glucose after 5 minutes.

(d) Enzyme X can only remove glucose from a free chain end. Because polymer B is branched, each molecule has 40 chain ends, compared with only 1 for polymer L. With many more ends available, many enzyme X molecules can remove glucose from polymer B at the same time, so glucose is released faster in Tube 2 than in Tube 1.

bonds_L = monomers - 1
assert bonds_L == 1199
water_needed = bonds_L * 1
assert water_needed == 1199
ends_L = 1
ends_B = 40
assert ends_B > ends_L
assert ends_B // ends_L == 40
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

item.title: Branching and Glucose Release from Two Polysaccharides
item.stimulus:
A student compares two polysaccharides, L and B. Both are polymers built only from glucose monomers. Polymer L is an unbranched (linear) chain. Polymer B is highly branched, so it has many more chain ends than polymer L. The student adds the same enzyme to 1.0 mg samples of each polymer under identical conditions. The enzyme acts only at chain ends, removing one glucose monomer at a time from the end of a chain. The student measures the initial rate of glucose release.

Polymer | Relative number of chain ends (per mg) | Initial rate of glucose release (µmol/min)
L (linear) | 1 | 12
B (branched) | 5 | 60
item.model_answer:
(a) The enzyme catalyzes hydrolysis. A water molecule is added across the covalent bond that links the last glucose monomer to the chain, breaking the bond and releasing a free glucose monomer.

(b) Rate for B ÷ rate for L = 60 µmol/min ÷ 12 µmol/min = 5. Polymer B releases glucose 5 times faster than polymer L.

(c) Because polymer B is branched, each milligram has many more chain ends, and the enzyme can act only at chain ends. More ends means more enzyme molecules can remove glucose at the same time. The data support this: polymer B has 5 times as many chain ends as polymer L and releases glucose 5 times as fast.

(d) The total amount of glucose will be the same. Both polymers are made only of glucose monomers, and both samples have the same mass (1.0 mg), so they contain the same number of glucose units. Branching changes only how the monomers are arranged and connected, which changes how quickly glucose can be removed, not how much glucose is present.
item.verification_python:
from fractions import Fraction
rate_L = 12
rate_B = 60
ends_L = 1
ends_B = 5
ratio = Fraction(rate_B, rate_L)
assert ratio == 5
assert Fraction(ends_B, ends_L) == ratio
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')
